title: The Iran War at Six Months: A Region—and Its Relationship With the U.S.—Transformed | Council on Foreign Relations
gist: Six months after the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran on February 28, 2026 and killed Supreme Leader Khamenei, a CFR expert roundup argues the war has left Washington facing strategic defeat, opened a new chapter of Iran-inspired online extremism, boosted Turkey regardless of outcome, cemented U.S.-Israel military ties amid falling political support, and reshaped Gulf security via the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement and the Abraham Accords. Compromised navigation through the Strait of Hormuz and a fragile ceasefire leave the region transformed but unstable.

themes.theme: U.S. strategic defeat and economic pressure

insights.claim: On February 28, 2026, the United States and Israel attacked Iran, killing Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei and targeting Iran's nuclear and military infrastructure, followed by a Pakistan-mediated ceasefire and June memorandum of understanding that halted large-scale fighting.
insights.speaker: Steven A. Cook
insights.so_what: The decapitation strike and fragile MoU frame the entire regional risk map; the June MoU is the ceasefire anchor whose breach would reignite conflict.
insights.locator: On February 28, 2026, the United States and Israel attacked Iran

insights.claim: Trump expected Operation Epic Fury to secure victory in four to six weeks but underestimated Iran's willingness to resist, leaving freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz greatly compromised and Gulf partners vulnerable to Iranian attack—a strategic defeat for Washington if not reversed.
insights.speaker: Steven A. Cook
insights.so_what: A CFR expert framing the outcome as U.S. strategic defeat signals durable regional-risk and shipping-lane premia, not a resolved conflict.
insights.quote: These are significant setbacks and represent a strategic defeat for Washington if they are not reversed.
insights.locator: Trump's Iran Miscalculation Leaves U.S. Confronting Strategic Defeat

insights.claim: The incentive for Tehran to weaponize its nuclear program, or what is left of it, is now greater than ever after six months of war.
insights.speaker: Steven A. Cook
insights.so_what: The strikes may have raised, not lowered, proliferation risk—a tail risk for the region and for any future negotiation.
insights.quote: the incentive for Tehran to weaponize its nuclear program (or what is left of it) is greater than ever
insights.locator: Trump's Iran Miscalculation Leaves U.S. Confronting Strategic Defeat

insights.claim: Trump's bet that economic pain via Operation Economic Outcast will collapse the Iranian regime overstates its effect, since Iranians' economic situation has been bad for years and the regime has shown willingness to kill and arrest citizens who protested in December 2025 and January 2026.
insights.speaker: Steven A. Cook
insights.so_what: Sanctions-led regime change is unlikely on this analysis; the stalemate—and its oil-price and security overhang—persists longer than markets may assume.
insights.quote: the economic situation for most Iranians has been bad for years and has only gotten worse since the beginning of the war
insights.locator: By pursuing Operation Economic Outcast

themes.theme: New chapter of Iran-inspired online extremism

insights.claim: The U.S.-Israeli war has given Iran and its proxies a fresh opening to radicalize and recruit global youth through well-timed, sophisticated online propaganda using memes, videos, and social media aimed at soft targets like infrastructure and synagogues.
insights.speaker: Steven A. Cook
insights.so_what: Extremism risk is now a homeland-security and soft-target exposure that persists independent of the battlefield ceasefire.
insights.locator: The Iran War Has Opened New Chapter of Extremism

insights.claim: Iran's six-month content advantage will encourage individuals not formally tied to it to act, including attempted assassinations of public figures and homeland violence, with youth and criminals engaged through cash incentives.
insights.speaker: Steven A. Cook
insights.so_what: Lone-actor and pay-for-violence risk against symbolic and U.S./Israel-linked business targets is elevated and durable.
insights.quote: creating a dangerous content advantage that will encourage individuals to act even if they are not formally associated with Iran or its proxies
insights.locator: Indeed, Iran has demonstrated six months of successful storytelling

insights.claim: Even if hostilities cease immediately, so much extremist content has been generated that the damage from the war will reverberate for years, opening a new chapter in violent extremism for which the U.S. is unprepared.
insights.speaker: Steven A. Cook
insights.so_what: A ceasefire will not clear the extremism overhang—budget and threat exposure to counter-radicalization runs well past any peace deal.
insights.quote: the events of the last six months, showcased on small phone screens in every possible manner, have opened a new chapter in violent extremism
insights.locator: Even if hostilities cease tomorrow

insights.claim: Turkey benefits from the Iran war regardless of outcome: a U.S. defeat boosts Ankara's standing as a regional counterweight, while a defeat of the ayatollahs and regime change in Iran would open new economic avenues for Turkey by removing its primary rival.
insights.speaker: Steven A. Cook
insights.so_what: Turkey is the structural winner of the regional realignment—position for expanding Turkish influence across defense and economic ties.
insights.quote: Paradoxically, Ankara benefits regardless of the war's outcome.
insights.locator: With Iran War, Turkey Wins Regardless of Who Prevails

insights.claim: The Mecca Joint Defense Agreement signed by Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Turkey on August 7, 2026 formally incorporates Turkey into a regional security alliance—the first such arrangement since the 1955 Baghdad Pact.
insights.speaker: Steven A. Cook
insights.so_what: A new Gulf security architecture is forming that pulls Turkey in and hedges away from sole U.S. reliance—track it as a marker of declining U.S. primacy.
insights.locator: The Mecca Joint Defense Agreement

insights.claim: Trump has signaled a break from Washington's long-standing reluctance to let Ankara play an autonomous regional role, envisioning that increased Turkish clout could help reduce the U.S. military presence in the Middle East.
insights.speaker: Steven A. Cook
insights.so_what: A U.S.-Turkey handoff of regional burden could accelerate American drawdown—relevant to defense-posture and Gulf-security exposure.
insights.locator: Even before the war, Trump had envisioned

themes.theme: U.S.-Israel military ties vs falling political support

insights.claim: The 2026 conflict cemented IDF-CENTCOM collaboration to one of the most extensive levels since the U.S.-UK alliance in World War II, with dozens of U.S. Air Force planes based in Israel, shared targeting data on Iran, and U.S. tankers refueling Israeli combat jets.
insights.speaker: Steven A. Cook
insights.so_what: Military integration is deepening even as politics frays—defense cooperation is the durable layer of the relationship.
insights.quote: This is one of the most extensive patterns of military cooperation since the alliance between the United States and the United Kingdom during World War II.
insights.locator: U.S.-Israel Military Ties as Tight as Ever

insights.claim: Opinion polls suggest U.S. support for Israel has declined substantially among both major political parties, feeding preexisting antisemitic and anti-Israel forces amid claims Israel lured the U.S. into war with Iran.
insights.speaker: Steven A. Cook
insights.so_what: Eroding bipartisan support is a slow structural risk to U.S.-Israel policy continuity over the longer horizon.
insights.quote: support for Israel has declined substantially among both major political parties in the United States
insights.locator: Opinion polls suggest that support for Israel

insights.claim: A key U.S.-Israel fault line is strategic aim: Washington seeks to change the Iranian regime's behavior on nuclear weapons and the Strait of Hormuz, while Israel sees regime change as the only real option, making any U.S.-Iran compromise a source of discord.
insights.speaker: Steven A. Cook
insights.so_what: The behavior-change vs regime-change split means Israel could act as a spoiler to any negotiated de-escalation.
insights.locator: The U.S. goal now is to force a change

themes.theme: Iran's proxy war via criminal cut-outs

insights.claim: Rather than deploy Hezbollah or IRGC Quds Force operatives directly, Iran has relied on pay-for-hire criminals recruited online and expatriates to obscure its hand behind unsophisticated attacks—arson, incendiary devices, vehicular rammings, stabbings, and some bombings.
insights.speaker: Steven A. Cook
insights.so_what: A deniable, low-cost proxy model raises attribution difficulty and broadens the target set—harder to deter, easier to sustain.
insights.quote: Iran has relied on a variegated collection of pay-for-hire criminals, often recruited online
insights.locator: Iran's Proxies War

insights.claim: A previously unknown group calling itself HAYI claimed eighteen attacks across Europe and London in March and April, with two Jewish men seriously wounded in an April knife attack in London's Golders Green; British authorities believe the IRGC and Quds Force are behind the incidents.
insights.speaker: Steven A. Cook
insights.so_what: Concrete European attack tally shows the proxy campaign is already operational abroad—elevated risk to Jewish and Israel-linked targets in Europe.
insights.locator: In Europe, for instance, a previously unknown group

insights.claim: The Iranian-backed Foxtrot Network, a violence-as-a-service (VaaS) organized-crime group, is believed responsible for three-dozen murders since 2022 plus attacks on Israeli targets in Europe, recruiting teenage operatives paid in cash and abandoned if caught.
insights.speaker: Steven A. Cook
insights.so_what: The VaaS model industrializes deniable violence and is unlikely to abate, especially if the war escalates—persistent European security risk.
insights.quote: Law enforcement authorities describe the network as a “violence-as-a-service” or VaaS criminal enterprise
insights.locator: It is also worth noting that, since 2022

themes.theme: Gulf realignment and a safer-for-now Arabian Peninsula

insights.claim: Iran has repeatedly attacked every Arab Gulf state, isolating itself from Sunni Arabs, with the UAE sustaining more attacks than even Israel since the war started.
insights.speaker: Steven A. Cook
insights.so_what: Iran's aggression has collapsed any Gulf sympathy and pushed Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar, and the UAE closer to Washington—a realignment favoring U.S.-aligned Gulf security.
insights.quote: The United Arab Emirates (UAE) has come under particularly heavy fire, sustaining more attacks than even Israel since the war started.
insights.locator: Issues Remain, but Arabian Peninsula Is Safer Than Before

insights.claim: The Abraham Accords helped protect the skies of the UAE with an interception success rate above 90 percent against Iranian attacks.
insights.speaker: Steven A. Cook
insights.so_what: Air-defense integration under the Accords is delivering measurable protection—validating the alliance framework as regional security infrastructure.
insights.quote: those accords have helped protect the skies of the UAE with an interception success rate above 90 percent
insights.locator: As Iran's clerical regime has attacked civilian infrastructure

insights.claim: The Arabian Peninsula is safer today with a defanged and denuclearized Iran, with the two remaining immediate concerns being the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen and control of the Strait of Hormuz.
insights.speaker: Steven A. Cook
insights.so_what: A contrarian read among CFR experts—some see net Gulf security improvement, with the Houthis and Hormuz as the residual watch items.
insights.quote: there is no doubt the Arabian Peninsula is safer today with a defanged and denuclearized Iran—for now
insights.locator: Two issues remain of immediate concern

insights.claim: Lebanon's government is the most promising regional actor, asserting sovereignty after decades of ceding it to Hezbollah, but Israel's continued presence in the south and an air campaign that killed thousands and displaced one million more limit its recovery.
insights.speaker: Steven A. Cook
insights.so_what: Lebanese sovereignty and Hezbollah disarmament are an over-the-horizon but possible path—an upside case gated by Israeli operations.
insights.locator: The Lebanese government remains the most promising actor

insights.claim: After the 2024 fall of Assad dealt Iran a crucial setback, Ahmed al-Sharaa's Syrian government has spent eighteen months building institutions and distancing Damascus from Tehran, but Syria remains fragile with ISIS holdouts and a lingering Iran-aligned network.
insights.speaker: Steven A. Cook
insights.so_what: Syria's pivot away from Iran is a structural regional shift, but ISIS and Iran-aligned remnants keep the recovery vulnerable.
insights.locator: The fall of Syrian President Bashar al-Assad's regime in 2024
